clue.text: Everything's OK, if you're Cratchit's nephew?

definitions.meaning: a breezy British catchphrase meaning all is done and fine
Bob Cratchit, the clerk in Dickens's A Christmas Carol, would be the uncle of any nephew of his, so the phrase is literally true for that child

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether all is well for a relative of Dickens's downtrodden clerk.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a British idiom for 'and there you are, job done', said when something turns out simply.

clue.text: Make it as artist, concealing unpopular name in islands

parts.note: to make it as something is to be that thing, so the phrase gives BE

indicators.note: concealing means hiding inside, so the artist holds the next piece

parts.note: RA, a Royal Academician, is the stock crossword artist
from the idiom 'your name is mud', said of someone in disgrace

explanation.surface: Someone tries to succeed as a painter in an island setting while hiding a bad reputation.
explanation.definitionFit: Bermuda is a British territory made up of many small islands in the Atlantic.

clue.text: Grandiose clubs with a lot of money and wine

parts.note: a bomb is British slang for a fortune, as in 'cost a bomb'
Asti is a sparkling Italian wine
C is the card-suit abbreviation for clubs

explanation.surface: Showy golf clubs are bought with plenty of cash and some wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' and 'and' just join; the clubs' C goes at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Bombastic speech is pompous and inflated, high-sounding without substance.

clue.text: The old way to conceal a rising agent

indicators.note: to conceal something is to hold it inside, so the letter A goes within the pieces

parts.note: ye is an archaic form of 'the'
ST, street, is a common abbreviation for a way

explanation.surface: An old way of hiding an agent who is being promoted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rising agent' sounds like a spy on the up; it is what makes dough rise.
explanation.definitionFit: Yeast is the fungus that makes bread dough rise by producing gas.

clue.text: Common way to refer to painting?

definitions.text: Common way to refer to painting?

parts.words: Common way to refer to painting?
parts.note: reads like the usual way to name a picture, but plays on common as 'not of the nobility', like a canvas with no name at all

explanation.surface: A question about the usual way of naming a picture.
explanation.definitionFit: A commoner holds no title, and a picture with no name is labelled the same way in catalogues.

clue.text: Cheerful gesture made by director at end of bar

definitions.text: gesture made by director at end of bar
definitions.meaning: a conductor's upward beat marking the last beat of a musical bar

explanation.surface: A film director makes a happy gesture at the end of a pub counter.
explanation.definitionFit: In music the upward stroke of a conductor's baton marks the unaccented last beat; the word also means optimistic.

clue.text: Message from a British member taken by force

indicators.note: pieces taken by another are held inside it

parts.note: to cram is to force or stuff in
a leg is a limb, a member of the body

explanation.surface: A British MP's message is seized by force.
explanation.definitionFit: A cablegram was a telegram sent by undersea cable, a message.

clue.text: Moderates improve a session, taking part

indicators.note: only a part of the words is taken, so the answer lies inside them

explanation.surface: Moderates in politics improve a meeting by joining in.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across improvE A SESsion.
explanation.definitionFit: To ease something is to lessen or moderate it; the verb forms match.

clue.text: Lie, say, in part of building

indicators.note: say tells us the word is to be spoken, its spelling changed

parts.note: a story is a fib, a lie

explanation.surface: Someone tells a lie inside part of a building.
explanation.definitionFit: A storey is one level or floor of a building.

clue.text: Unrestrained tirade interrupted by a politician

indicators.note: a speech interrupted by someone has that person breaking into its middle, so the second pieces go inside

parts.note: a tirade is a rant
MP, Member of Parliament, is the standard crossword politician

explanation.surface: An angry harangue is cut into by an MP.
explanation.definitionFit: Rampant means running wild, unchecked, as unrestrained growth or behaviour is.

clue.text: Take responsibility for a small charge

definitions.text: Take responsibility for a small charge

parts.words: Take responsibility for a small charge
parts.note: reads like accepting a minor fee or accusation, but the small charge is a child left in one's care for an evening

explanation.surface: Someone accepts the blame for a minor fee or offence.
explanation.definitionFit: Minding a little child while the parents are out is the job, the child being a charge in the sense of a ward.

clue.text: Put an eccentric out of place

indicators.note: eccentric means odd or off-centre, telling us these letters are set in an odd new order

explanation.surface: An oddball is told to put something where it does not belong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eccentric' looks like a noun for an oddball, but it signals the anagram of PUTAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Unapt means unsuitable or inappropriate, which is what something misplaced is.

clue.text: Farcical author king makes crosser?

parts.note: Ben Travers wrote the famous Aldwych farces of the 1920s
ER stands for Edwardus Rex, King Edward

explanation.surface: A writer of farces teams up with a monarch to make someone angrier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crosser' looks like 'more annoyed', but it means one who crosses; the question mark flags the coined noun.
explanation.definitionFit: One who traverses something goes across it, so is literally someone who crosses.

clue.text: During trial, top journalist gave evidence

parts.note: at as in 'at the time of', i.e. during
a test is a trial
ED, short for editor, the senior journalist on a paper

explanation.surface: A senior newspaperman testified in the course of a court case.
explanation.definitionFit: To attest is to bear witness or certify formally, as a witness does in court.

clue.text: Source of a fruit badly needed in South America?

definitions.text: Source of a fruit badly needed in South America?

indicators.note: pieces needed in something go inside it, here inside the abbreviation

parts.note: a pod is a fruit in the botanical sense, as on peas
ill means badly, as in 'ill-treated'

explanation.surface: A fruit that South America sorely lacks.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines a tropical American tree and also builds it.
explanation.definitionFit: The sapodilla is a tropical American evergreen that bears sweet brown fruit and yields chicle.

clue.text: Literary savage whose child has positive qualities

definitions.meaning: The islander rescued by the hero in Defoe's Robinson Crusoe, called a savage in the novel
in the old nursery rhyme the child born on this weekday is 'loving and giving'

explanation.surface: A character from a novel is a parent whose offspring is very good-natured.
explanation.definitionFit: The weekday names Crusoe's companion and appears in the rhyme beginning 'Monday's child is fair of face'.

clue.text: Underworld agent with appearance of total neglect

parts.note: Dis is the Roman god of the underworld, and the underworld itself
a rep is a sales agent
an air is a look or appearance

explanation.surface: A spy from hell has a look of complete neglect.
explanation.definitionFit: Disrepair is the state of a building fallen into ruin from neglect.

clue.text: Fortress's; foundation incorporating boulder clay

definitions.note: read as 'Fortress is', the 's being the link

indicators.note: incorporating means taking into its body, so the clay goes inside

parts.note: a base is a foundation
till is a geologist's term for clay mixed with boulders left by glaciers

explanation.surface: A fortress has foundations built into boulder clay.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of 'Fortress's' stands for 'is', joining definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bastille was the Paris fortress-prison stormed in 1789.

clue.text: Prescription price adjusted to cover drug

indicators.note: one piece covering another surrounds it, so the drug goes inside the rearranged letters
adjusted means altered, so the letters of the word price are reordered

parts.note: E is short for ecstasy, the standard crossword drug

explanation.surface: A pharmacist raises the cost charged to pay for a medicine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'adjusted' rearranges PRICE to RCIPE, and 'to cover' puts E inside it after the R.
explanation.definitionFit: A recipe was originally a doctor's written instruction, the Latin 'take', the source of the Rx symbol on prescriptions.

clue.text: Reflective type upset over English summary

indicators.note: in a down clue upset means turned upside down, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a muser is someone who reflects

explanation.surface: A thoughtful person is upset by an English summary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' places the reversed MUSER above E in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A résumé is a brief summing-up of something.

clue.text: Monkey put next to tailless rodent

indicators.note: an animal without its tail loses its end, so the last letter is cut

parts.note: a marmot is a large burrowing rodent
to set something is to put it down

explanation.surface: A primate is placed beside a rodent that has lost its tail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'next to' just places SET after the shortened rodent.
explanation.definitionFit: The marmoset is a small South American monkey with a long tail.

clue.text: Cobblers from East End walk in a funny way

indicators.note: end means the last letter of the preceding word

parts.note: to waddle is to walk with a comic rolling gait

explanation.surface: Shoemakers from London's East End walk with a strange gait.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cobblers' is British slang for nonsense, from rhyming slang; East End evokes Cockney London but gives just T.
explanation.definitionFit: Twaddle and cobblers are both everyday British words for nonsense.

clue.text: Uncommunicative, like bishop, initially, when in doubt?

definitions.text: like bishop, initially, when in doubt?
definitions.meaning: the first letter of bishop is B, and the B in the word doubt is not pronounced

explanation.surface: A bishop gone quiet when unsure of his faith.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying nothing is being mute, and a letter not pronounced is called mute too.

clue.text: Deposit frozen in a bank?

parts.note: reads like money locked in an account, but the deposit is snow piled by wind and the bank is a heap of it

explanation.surface: Someone's savings have been frozen by their bank.
explanation.definitionFit: Wind-driven snow settles in banks against walls and hedges, a frozen deposit indeed.

clue.text: Old island accommodating a saint's resting-place

indicators.note: accommodating means housing, so the old island holds the next pieces

explanation.surface: An ancient island houses a saint's tomb.
explanation.definitionFit: An oasis is a fertile watered spot in a desert where travellers rest.

clue.text: Sounds like friendly greeting to girl one's spotted, perhaps

indicators.note: tells us the answer is said the same way as the phrase that follows

parts.note: Hi! said to a girl called Ena, giving HI ENA

explanation.surface: A man calls a cheerful hello to a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one's spotted' means 'one is spotted'; 'perhaps' because only some kinds of this animal have spots.
explanation.definitionFit: The spotted hyena is the best-known species of the African scavenger, its coat dotted with dark marks.

clue.text: Large animal taking fruit on river

parts.note: a hip is the fruit of the rose
the Po is the great river of northern Italy

explanation.surface: A big beast eats fruit by a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' sets HIP above PO in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: The hippo is a huge African river mammal.

clue.text: After months in Paris, she produces wine

indicators.note: after places the French word behind the abbreviation for months

parts.note: MOS is an abbreviation of months
elle is French for she

explanation.surface: A Parisian woman makes wine after some months.
explanation.definitionFit: Moselle is white wine from the valley of the river of that name in Germany and France.

clue.text: Young fellow framing map of European region

indicators.note: a frame goes round a picture, so the lad surrounds the map

parts.note: a lad is a young fellow
a plan is a map or drawing

explanation.surface: A boy puts a map of part of Europe in a frame.
explanation.definitionFit: Lapland is the far northern region of Scandinavia and Finland, home of the Sami.

clue.text: Suspension indelicate people, say, endure to the end

parts.note: a stay is a suspension, as in a stay of execution

indicators.note: say signals that the phrase is to be heard rather than spelt

parts.note: the coarse, crude folk taken as a group

explanation.surface: Vulgar folk are told to put up with a suspension.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' makes 'the coarse' a homophone of 'the course'.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep going in a race or task until it is finished is to last the full distance.
